what_it_does: Graph processing — computing things like shortest paths or influence scores across millions or billions of connected nodes (think the entire web or a social network at scale) — requires keeping track of a 'state' value for every node. Existing hardware accelerators for this work by loading a chunk (partition) of nodes into the chip's fast on-chip memory, processing them, writing results back to the large slow off-chip memory chip (DRAM), then loading the next chunk — repeating many times. This repeated loading and flushing wastes bandwidth and limits how big a graph you can handle efficiently. NOVA separates two operations that existing designs interleave — 'reduce' (collecting incoming updates to a node) and 'propagate' (sending a node's updated value to its neighbors) — which allows the entire node-state table to live in DRAM permanently rather than being shuttled on and off chip. The small on-chip memory acts purely as a staging buffer to hide DRAM's latency (the delay between asking for data and receiving it), not as a storage location. Multiple NOVA chips can be linked together to handle larger graphs with near-linear scaling.
